fetched_contents.text: Remdesivir in pregnant women with moderate to severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19): a retrospective cohort study Abstract Data on the efficacy of remdesivir in Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) are limited in pregnant patients since they have been excluded from clinical trials. We aimed to investigate some clinical outcomes following remdesivir administration in pregnancy. This was a retrospective cohort study conducted on pregnant women with moderate to severe COVID-19. The enrolled patients were divided into two groups with and without remdesivir treatment. The primary outcomes of this study were the length of hospital and intensive care unit stay; respiratory parameters of hospital day 7 including respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and mode of oxygen support; discharge until days 7 and 14, and need for home oxygen therapy. Secondary outcomes included some maternal and neonatal consequences. Eighty-one pregnant women (57 in the remdesivir group and 24 in the non-remdesivir group) were included. The two study groups were comparable according to the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics. Of the respiratory outcomes, remdesivir was significantly associated with a reduced length of hospital stay (p = 0.021) and also with a lower level of oxygen requirement in patients on low-flow oxygen [odds ratio (OR) 3.669]. Among the maternal consequences, no patients in the remdesivir group developed preeclampsia but three patients (12.5%) experienced this complication in the non-remdesivir group (p = 0.024). Furthermore, in patients with moderate COVID-19, the percentage of emergency termination was significantly lower in remdesivir group (OR 2.46). Our results demonstrated some probable benefits of remdesivir in respiratory and also maternal outcomes. Further investigations with a larger sample size should confirm these results. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10238-023-01095-0. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, several pharmacological treatments have been introduced using drug repurposing and have shown promising results for the treatment of moderate to severe cases [2]. SARS-CoV-2 uses RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) for replication, and remdesivir, a nucleotide analog, inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 replication via selective suppression of viral RdRp in vitro [3, 4]. Over the past 2 years, several studies and trials have demonstrated the efficacy of remdesivir treatment in non-pregnant adults with severe COVID-19 [5, 6]. However, studies such as the WHO Solidarity trial have reported that remdesivir had no effect on the length of hospital stay or survival compared with the standard of care [7]. Other trials have yielded equivocal results regarding the effects of remdesivir [8, 9]. Pregnant patients are more vulnerable to severe or critical features of COVID-19 [10]. For instance, the risk of intensive care unit (ICU) admission and the need for mechanical ventilation is approximately two to four times higher among pregnant than matched non-pregnant women [11–13]. Physiological changes in the immune and cardiovascular systems are probably the underlying reason for the increased susceptibility of pregnant women to viral respiratory infections [14]. The risk of severe disease increases especially when respiratory infection occurs in the third trimester [11–13, 15]. In addition, pregnancy outcomes could be impacted by COVID-19, resulting in the higher rates of preterm birth and cesarean section [16]. Data on the administration of remdesivir in COVID-19 pregnant patients are scarce since pregnant women have been excluded from clinical trials of remdesivir. Nonetheless, Remdesivir was authorized in pregnant women with severe COVID-19 as of March 21, 2020, through a compassionate-use program [10]. In this retrospective cohort study, we aimed to explore the association between remdesivir and pregnancy outcomes in patients with moderate to severe COVID-19. fetched_contents.text: Transplacental transfer of Remdesivir and GS‐441524: An ex vivo perfusion study 1. INTRODUCTION Remdesivir (Rmd) is a prodrug of GS‐441524 (GS) originally developed against Ebola, proven to reduce in vitro SARS‐Cov‐2 replication. 1 , 2 Pharmacokinetics (PK) data are few and show that Rmd is rapidely metabolized into GS. 3 Maximal Remdesivir concentrations (Cmax) and different PK exposure parameters have been reported according to different dosing regimen. 3 In healthy volunteers, a Cmax higher than 4000 ng/mL was found after an IV administration of 225 mg of Rmd. However, pregnant women were not included in this report. Several reviews reported the use of Rmd in pregnant women, 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 but did not analyse Rmd or GS concentration neither in mothers nor in cord blood. A physiological based PK model has been done to predict mother concentrations but without fetal concentrations. 8 Gilead's report suggested some reproductive toxicity in rats, 3 but no data regarding Rmd and its metabolite transfer through the placental was available. Being a large spectrum antiretroviral drug, Rmd can be given in any emerging RNA virus infection, and the lack of information regarding pregnant women may be a concern in drug dosing. Among the different methods to study the transplacental transfer of drugs, the closest to human physiology is the perfusion of the human cotyledon. 9 In the present study, we aimed to evaluate the transfer of Rmd and GS‐441524 in an ex vivo cotyledon perfusion model. 2. METHOD Placentas were obtained from women who delivered at Port Royal maternity, Paris, France. All patients received an information note and gave a written consent for this study, approved by the ethic board of Nord Ouest IV committee, and registered in clinicaltrial.gov (NCT04400084). We included women aged over 18 years, with social insurance, with a single pregnancy between 37 and 41 weeks of gestation, from April to June 2020. Patients with a chronic therapy or HIV, HBV or HCV infection, or with a pregnancy disorder, which likely induces modifications of the placenta vascularization, or with fetal growth delay, were not included. Cotyledons were perfused within the hour following the delivery in double closed circuit, for 3 h (see supplemental data). 10 Antipyrine (Sigma, Acros Organics Society) and Rmd (purchased from Gilead in march 2020) were added at the beginning of the perfusion into the maternal compartment, at 20 mg/L 11 and 4000 ng/mL, respectively. 3 No GS was added. Samples from the maternal and fetal compartments were collected throughout the 3 h of perfusion and stored at −30°C until analysis. Antipyrine, our control molecule, was first quantified by liquid chromatography, and the standard validation criteria were calculated: fetal to mother concentration ratio and a fetal transfer rate (FTR), which is a ratio of drug quantity transferred to the fetus to the total quantity (from both sides) at the end of the experiment (see supplemental data). 11 A perfusion is validated when the ratio is ≥75% and the FTR ≥ 20%. Then Rmd and GS of the validated perfusions were quantified by a mass spectrometry detection (Xevo TQD, Waters®) (see supplemental data). A FTR at 3 h was calculated using the same formula as for antipyrine. Categorical data were summarized and presented as frequencies and percentages. Continuous data were presented as median (Inter quartile range [IQR]) (range). Statistical descriptive analysis was performed on R software (http://cran.r-project.org/). 3. RESULTS From the 19 women included, 10 placentas were successfully perfused during 3 h. Only eight perfusions were validated with antipyrine our control molecule, from women aged between 29 and 39 years, who gave birth to four girls and four boys born by vaginal delivery. Population characteristics are presented in the Supporting Information: Table S1. As shown in Figure 1, Rmd decreased rapidly in the maternal compartment, from around 4000 ng/mL to a mean concentration of 867 ng/mL after 3 h of perfusion (Table 1). But the fetal Rmd concentrations rose up only to a median of 170 ng/mL at 3 h. fetched_contents.text: Remdesivir for the treatment of COVID‐19 in pregnancy PEER REVIEW The peer review history for this article is available at https://publons.com/publon/10.1002/jmv.26986 1. The devastating coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) global pandemic caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2) was declared by the World Health Organisation (WHO) in March 2020 and now at over 9 months since its declaration, it continues to claim vast numbers of lives all over the world. 1 There is no evidence that pregnant women are more susceptible to SARS‐CoV‐2 infection than the general population; however, pregnancy‐associated immunological changes could potentially render pregnant individuals more vulnerable to severe COVID‐19 as has been previously observed with influenza A/H1N1, severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) and middle east respiratory syndrome (MERS). 2 Evidence from the United States (US) cohort study suggests that severe COVID‐19 in pregnancy (predominantly in the third trimester) is associated with iatrogenic‐associated preterm birth (75% delivered preterm). 3 Data from the UK cohort study of 427 pregnant women hospitalised with COVID‐19 estimated an incidence of admission to hospital with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 infection of 4.9 per 1000 maternities. 2 In this study, 81% were in the third trimester or peripartum also suggesting that severe illness may be more common later in pregnancy. Ten percent (41/427) needed Level 3 critical care, of whom 80% (33/41) delivered their child while admitted with COVID‐19 (66% delivered due to worsening respiratory condition). Overall mortality in pregnant women admitted with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2 infection was 1.2% (5/427; three of whom died directly from complications of COVID‐19). COVID‐19 is responsible for a significant disease burden among pregnant women and although this may not be in excess of that observed in the general population, potential treatment options are limited even further in pregnant women, in part through their exclusion (often for justifiable reasons) from clinical trials. A review of COVID‐19 treatment studies (of nonbiological drugs) at two specific time points (April 7–20, 2020 and July 10–15, 2020) found that pregnant women were excluded from 80% and 75% of studies during the first and second time points, respectively. 4 Remdesivir (GS‐5734), an inhibitor of the viral RNA‐dependent RNA polymerase was identified as a potential candidate for the treatment of COVID‐19 after it was demonstrated to inhibit SARS‐CoV‐2 replication in vitro. 5 , 6 In a large multicentre, international double‐blind, randomised, placebo‐controlled trial of 1062 patients with COVID‐19 with evidence of lower respiratory tract infection, intravenous remdesivir (for 10 days or until hospital discharge or death) was associated with a shortened time to recovery when compared with placebo (median recovery time of 10 days with remdesivir vs. 15 days with placebo, p < 0.001) and remdesivir was also associated with a shortened time to discharge from hospital. 6 All‐cause mortality was 11.4% with remdesivir and 15.2% with placebo. Adverse events occurred in 24.6% of the remdesivir group and 31.6% of the placebo group. This study excluded pregnant and breast‐feeding women. A recent systematic review of remdesivir in hospitalised COVID‐19 patients found that remdesivir significantly increased the recovery rate (by 22% and 14% on Days 7 and 28, respectively) compared to the control group, and significantly reduced 14‐day mortality (by 36%) among moderate and severe COVID‐19 patients but there was no significant difference in 28‐day mortality. 7 Remdesivir has been the first drug to be approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States (Emergency Use Authorisation was first granted on May 1, 2020) for use in children and adults hospitalised with COVID‐19 and has also been approved in several other parts of the world. Pregnant women, however, are excluded from many recommendations for the use of remdesivir in COVID‐19 largely due to a lack of clinical trial data. Its administration in pregnancy has primarily been on a compassionate use basis. fetched_contents.text: Remdesivir for pregnancy: A systematic review of antiviral therapy for COVID-19 Abstract Objective The use of remdesivir for pregnant patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) showed conflicting results in prior studies. We aimed to systematically review its efficacy and safety for this population from the existing literature. Methods On July 26, 2021, registries (ClinicalTrials.gov) and databases (MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, JSTOR, DOAJ, and medRxiv) were systematically searched for research articles investigating remdesivir use in pregnant people with COVID-19. Clinical outcome, hospitalization duration, laboratory outcome, mortality, and adverse events were investigated. Results We obtained 13 observation studies with 113 pregnant people. In these studies, remdesivir improved the clinical condition of pregnant patients with COVID-19, especially those who had a better clinical status at baseline and received earlier remdesivir treatment. Most fetuses were delivered via cesarean section, primarily because of emergency causes. No vertical transmissions were noted. The most reported adverse event was transaminitis, in which 10-day remdesivir treatment yielded more incidence than the 5-day treatment. Conclusions In pregnancy, the use of Remdesivir in combination with other COVID-19 treatments is inconclusive but its use should be followed with careful monitoring of adverse reactions and transaminase enzyme levels. Further studies are required to confirm its finding. Observed maternal and neonatal outcomes in hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 receiving remdesivir

The evidence base for remdesivir in pregnant hospitalized patients with COVID-19 is primarily observational and limited by small sample sizes and lack of randomized controlled trials. In one retrospective cohort study of 81 pregnant women with moderate to severe COVID-19, remdesivir was associated with some favorable outcomes, including reduced length of hospital stay and lower oxygen requirement in patients on low-flow oxygen, and no development of preeclampsia in the remdesivir group versus 12.5% in the non-remdesivir group [N1-F1]. However, the study did not report specific rates of preterm birth, stillbirth, or other pregnancy-specific adverse events in the remdesivir arm alone, so those outcomes are not directly observed from this source [N1-F1].

Neonatal outcomes are similarly sparse in the direct evidence. A separate case series mentions a baby born to a mother treated with remdesivir who had a birth weight of 2.3 kg and Apgar scores of 9 and 10, but this is one case and not a representative outcome measure [N2-R1]. Other sources report broader neonatal risks associated with maternal COVID-19 infection in pregnancy, such as preterm birth, low birth weight, and poor Apgar scores, but these are general associations rather than remdesivir-specific effects [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. A larger US cohort study of 64 hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 reported that 25% received remdesivir, but the evidence provided does not include detailed neonatal outcomes for the remdesivir group [N4-R1]. A systematic review of antiviral therapy in pregnancy also noted that most fetuses were delivered via cesarean section primarily because of emergency causes, and no vertical transmission was noted, but it did not report remdesivir-specific neonatal outcomes [N5-F3].

For maternal outcomes, the evidence is more concrete. In the retrospective cohort study, remdesivir was associated with reduced hospital stay and lower oxygen requirement, and no preeclampsia was reported in the remdesivir group [N1-F1]. A broader cohort study of hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 found that severe disease was associated with ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and poor outcomes in general, with 41/427 women requiring Level 3 critical care and 80% of them delivering while admitted [N4-F2]. The same source also reported an overall mortality rate of 1.2% among hospitalized pregnant women with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection [N4-F2]. A compassionate-use report of 86 pregnant and postpartum women with severe COVID-19 noted high recovery rates and a low rate of serious adverse events, but it did not provide a detailed breakdown of ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, or mortality [N6-R2]. Thus, while remdesivir may have some favorable effects on respiratory and short-term maternal outcomes, the evidence for ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and mortality is indirect or limited to broader hospitalized pregnant cohorts rather than remdesivir-treated subgroups [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Overall, the reported outcomes are mixed: remdesivir appears associated with some improvement in respiratory and early maternal outcomes, but the evidence does not support strong conclusions about preterm birth, stillbirth, or specific neonatal adverse events in the remdesivir-treated group. The neonatal evidence is dominated by general associations with maternal infection and limited remdesivir-specific data [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
Safety and evidence quality of remdesivir use in pregnancy and lactation

The safety and evidence quality for remdesivir use in pregnancy and lactation are modestly reassuring but still limited. The placental transfer evidence is important: an ex vivo cotyledon perfusion study found that remdesivir (Rmd) does not pass through the blood-placental barrier, but its main active metabolite, GS-441524 (GS), remains in the maternal compartment. In that study, Rmd concentrations in the fetal compartment were low, with a fetal/maternal ratio of 0.22 and a fetal transfer rate (FTR) of 8.15% at 3 hours, while GS concentrations were also low and the placental transfer was weak overall [N3-F4]. This suggests that remdesivir is unlikely to cross the placenta in significant amounts, which is a relevant safety consideration. However, the study was ex vivo and not in human pregnancy, so it cannot fully substitute for clinical safety data [N3-F4].

Human safety evidence is limited and mostly observational. A systematic review of antiviral therapy in pregnancy reported that remdesivir use was associated with fewer adverse events, and in one 10-day treatment study, transaminitis was more common than in a 5-day regimen [N5-F3]. Another source noted that remdesivir appeared to be safe and well tolerated in a cohort with no recorded adverse reactions [N5-R2]. A compassionate-use report of 86 pregnant and postpartum women with severe COVID-19 also reported high recovery rates and a low rate of serious adverse events [N6-R2]. However, these studies are observational and lack randomized design, so they cannot rule out confounding or rare adverse events [N5-F3][N6-R2].

In contrast, the evidence base is very weak for controlled trials in pregnancy. The evidence provided does not include any randomized controlled trials of remdesivir in pregnant women with COVID-19, and most studies excluded pregnant women for justifiable reasons [N4-F2]. A review of remdesivir in hospitalized patients noted that it was associated with a shortened time to recovery and reduced 14-day mortality, but this was in non-pregnant patients [N4-F2]. The manufacturer’s Investigator’s Brochure also states that no reproductive developmental toxicity was observed in animals at clinically relevant doses, but this does not fully reassure human safety [N3-R2]. Overall, the safety evidence is reassuring in the sense that no large safety signals emerged in the limited human data, but the quality remains low because the evidence is observational and mostly based on compassionate use or small cohorts [N3-F4][N5-F3][N5-R2].

The evidence quality distinction is clear: pharmacokinetic and placental transfer evidence is direct and informative, but it is still experimental and not fully human-relevant [N3-F4]. Safety findings are mostly reassuring, but they come from observational studies rather than controlled trials, and they are therefore subject to selection bias and confounding [N5-F3][N5-R2]. Lactation evidence is not directly addressed in the provided materials, so it cannot be assessed here [N3-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Context for interpreting remdesivir use in hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19

The clinical context for remdesivir use in hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 is shaped by the lack of robust trial data and the increased vulnerability of pregnancy to severe disease. A broader cohort study of hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 found that severe disease was associated with ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and higher mortality than in nonpregnant women [N4-F2]. The same source also noted that 41/427 hospitalized pregnant women required Level 3 critical care, with 80% delivering while admitted, highlighting the urgency of treatment and the high-risk nature of severe maternal illness [N4-F2]. Remdesivir was used primarily on a compassionate-use basis because pregnant women were excluded from most clinical trials [N4-F2]. In a US cohort of 64 hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19, 25% received remdesivir, but the evidence provided does not provide detailed treatment rationale or standard-of-care comparison [N4-R1].

In terms of indications, remdesivir appears to be used when maternal illness is moderate to severe and when there is a clinical need for intervention, rather than as a standard-of-care option in pregnancy [N4-F2][N4-R1]. The compassionate-use reports indicate that remdesivir was considered for hospitalized pregnant women with severe disease, particularly those requiring supplemental oxygen [N6-R5]. In the retrospective cohort study, remdesivir was associated with reduced hospital stay and lower oxygen requirement, and the authors concluded that it demonstrated some probable benefits in respiratory and maternal outcomes [N1-F1]. However, the evidence quality is limited because the studies are observational, and the authors acknowledged the need for larger studies [N1-F1][N4-F2].

The risk-benefit tradeoff is therefore mixed. On the maternal side, remdesivir may help reduce hospital stay and improve respiratory status, which can be important for a pregnant woman with severe illness [N1-F1][N4-F2]. On the fetal/neonatal side, the evidence is less direct. The placental transfer study suggests limited placental exposure, which is reassuring, but the neonatal outcomes in the provided materials are mostly general associations with maternal infection rather than remdesivir-specific effects [N3-F4][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. The systematic review also noted that most fetuses were delivered via cesarean section primarily because of emergency causes, and no vertical transmission was noted, but it did not show remdesivir-specific benefit or harm [N5-F3].

Study limitations are substantial. The evidence is heavily observational, with small cohorts, lack of randomization, and potential for selection bias and confounding [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3]. The retrospective cohort study had no control group and relied on a small sample of 81 pregnant women [N1-F1]. The compassionate-use reports are also limited by their observational design and lack of comparator groups [N6-R2]. As a result, any observed benefit should be interpreted cautiously, and the evidence does not support strong conclusions about long-term safety or fetal/neonatal outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Summary

The evidence for remdesivir use in hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 is limited, observational, and mostly derived from compassionate use rather than controlled trials. The available data suggest some favorable short-term maternal outcomes, but the evidence for preterm birth, stillbirth, and specific neonatal adverse events is sparse or indirect. Overall, remdesivir appears associated with reduced hospital stay and improved respiratory status in some pregnant patients, but the outcomes are not sufficient to conclude broad safety or efficacy for pregnancy-specific adverse events [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Observed maternal outcomes

The most directly reported maternal outcomes in hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 who received remdesivir come from a retrospective cohort study of 81 pregnant women with moderate to severe COVID-19. In this study, remdesivir was associated with a reduced length of hospital stay and lower oxygen requirement in patients on low-flow oxygen [N1-F1]. Importantly, no patients in the remdesivir group developed preeclampsia, whereas 12.5% of patients in the non-remdesivir group did [N1-F1]. However, the study did not report specific rates of ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, or mortality for the remdesivir-treated group alone, so those outcomes cannot be confidently attributed to remdesivir [N1-F1].

In a broader hospitalized pregnant cohort, severe COVID-19 was associated with ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and poor outcomes, with 41/427 hospitalized pregnant women requiring Level 3 critical care and 80% delivering while admitted [N4-F2]. This context is important because it shows that maternal illness can be very severe, but it does not directly prove that remdesivir caused these outcomes or prevented them [N4-F2].

## Observed neonatal outcomes

The neonatal evidence is weaker and more indirect. A single case series mentions a baby born to a mother treated with remdesivir who had a birth weight of 2.3 kg and Apgar scores of 9 and 10, but this is one case and not representative of a larger pattern [N2-R1]. Other sources report general neonatal risks associated with maternal COVID-19 infection, such as preterm birth, low birth weight, and poor Apgar scores, but these are not remdesivir-specific findings [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. A systematic review of antiviral therapy in pregnancy also noted that most fetuses were delivered via cesarean section primarily because of emergency causes and that no vertical transmission was noted, but it did not report remdesivir-specific neonatal outcomes [N5-F3].

In short, the neonatal evidence supports the broader association between maternal COVID-19 infection and adverse neonatal outcomes, but the provided evidence does not support a strong conclusion that remdesivir itself caused or prevented specific neonatal adverse events [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N5-F3].

The safety and evidence quality for remdesivir use in pregnancy and lactation are modestly reassuring but still limited. This suggests limited placental exposure, which is relevant to safety, but the study was ex vivo and not in human pregnancy, so it cannot fully substitute for clinical safety data [N3-F4].

Human safety evidence is mostly observational and reassuring in a limited sense. A systematic review reported that remdesivir use was associated with fewer adverse events and that transaminitis was more common in a 10-day treatment study than in a 5-day regimen [N5-F3]. In hospitalized pregnant women with COVID-19 who received remdesivir, the observed outcomes are mixed.
